blocks.text: This topic goes deep into HTTP status codes relevant to LLM APIs, the full range from success through client errors to server errors, and critically, how to decide whether a specific status code warrants a retry, a fix to your own request, or an alert to a human.

This topic covers the 2xx, 4xx, and 5xx status code categories, the specific meanings of 400, 401, 403, 404, 422, 429, 500, and 503, and a practical framework for deciding whether each one warrants retrying, fixing your request, or escalating.
1. Status Codes as What Actually Happened

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Building on the response body, status codes tell you what actually happened

blocks.text: The HTTP status code returned with every response is the first, most authoritative signal of what actually happened with a request, before even looking at the response body content, checking this code first shapes how an application should handle everything that follows.
2. The Three Broad Categories

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: 2xx signals success, 4xx signals a client error, 5xx signals a server error

blocks.text: Status codes starting with 2 signal success, codes starting with 4 signal a problem with the request itself, something your application did wrong, codes starting with 5 signal a problem on the provider side, something the server itself failed at.

blocks.text: 3. 400 and 422, Malformed or Invalid Requests

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: 400 signals a malformed request, 422 signals an invalid parameter value

blocks.text: This connects directly to input validation and request body construction, both covered earlier, a 400 typically means the request itself is malformed, invalid JSON, a missing required field, a 422 more specifically means the request was well formed but contains an invalid value, a parameter outside its allowed range, both signal a bug in your own request, not something worth retrying unchanged.
4. 401 and 403, Authentication and Authorization

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: 401 means not authenticated, 403 means not authorized

blocks.text: This connects directly to authentication and API keys, both covered in an earlier module, a 401 means the request lacks valid credentials entirely, a missing or incorrect API key, a 403 means the credentials are valid but lack permission for this specific action, distinguishing these two helps pinpoint exactly what to fix.
5. 404, Resource Not Found

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: 404 means the resource was not found, often due to the wrong endpoint or resource ID

blocks.text: A 404 usually means the URL path itself is wrong, a typo in the endpoint, or a referenced resource ID, a specific stored file or configuration, that genuinely does not exist, this is worth checking against the provider actual documented endpoints rather than assuming a transient issue.
6. 429, Rate Limited

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: 429 means rate limited, warranting a retry after a delay

blocks.text: This connects directly to rate limiting, covered in an earlier module, a 429 specifically signals you have exceeded the allowed request rate, unlike most other 4xx codes, this genuinely does warrant a retry, but only after waiting an appropriate delay, often specified in a response header, rather than retrying immediately.

blocks.title: 429 is the clearest example of a 4xx code that should be retried
blocks.content: Unlike a 400 or 401, which indicate a genuine problem with the request that retrying unchanged will not fix, a 429 specifically means try again later, making it the one 4xx code where an automatic, delayed retry is usually the right response.

blocks.text: 7. 5xx, Server-Side Errors

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: 500 and 503 signal server errors, where a retry may genuinely help

blocks.text: A 500 indicates an internal error on the provider side, a 503 indicates the service is temporarily unavailable, both are outside your control and often transient, unlike most 4xx codes, retrying a 5xx after a brief delay is usually a reasonable strategy, since the underlying issue may resolve on the provider side.
8. A Practical Retry Decision Framework

A useful rule of thumb, 4xx codes other than 429 usually indicate a bug in your own request that retrying will not fix, requiring an actual code change, 429 and 5xx codes are worth retrying with an appropriate delay, since the underlying condition may resolve on its own, this connects directly to the retry mechanisms covered in the next topic.
9. A Worked Status Code Handling Example

A well built application checks the status code first, on 2xx it proceeds to parse the response body, on 429 or 5xx it retries with a delay, on any other 4xx it logs the specific error detail and surfaces it clearly rather than retrying blindly, treating each category according to what it genuinely signals.
Worked Example

A team initially retries every failed request identically regardless of status code, including 400 errors caused by a genuine bug in how they constructed a specific request parameter, resulting in the same failing request being retried repeatedly without ever succeeding, wasting time and API calls.

Adding explicit status code based handling, retrying only 429 and 5xx responses while immediately surfacing 400 and other client errors for investigation, both fixes the wasted retry loop and surfaces the actual underlying parameter bug far faster than the blind retry approach ever would have.
Common Mistakes

items: Retrying every failed request identically regardless of status code, wasting calls on errors retrying will never fix
Confusing 401, missing credentials, with 403, valid credentials lacking permission
Not respecting a retry delay hint when handling a 429 response, retrying too aggressively
Treating a 5xx server error the same as a 4xx client error, when the appropriate response genuinely differs

blocks.text: Practice

Write a status code handling function that takes a response status code and returns whether to retry, and if so how, versus surfacing an error immediately, covering at minimum 400, 401, 403, 429, and 500.
Key Takeaway

HTTP status codes are the first, most authoritative signal of what happened with a request, 4xx codes generally indicate a problem with the request itself worth fixing rather than retrying, except for 429 which specifically warrants a delayed retry, and 5xx codes indicate a provider side issue also worth retrying, distinguishing these categories correctly is what separates a robust application from one that wastes calls or misses a genuine bug.
